title: Are You Ready to Talk to Your Faculty, Students, and Parents About AGI?
author: Stefan Bauschard
summary: Stefan Bauschard argues that educational institutions have a responsibility to hold structured, evidence-based conversations about AGI now, rather than waiting for definitional consensus, given that OpenAI's Greg Brockman and Google DeepMind's Demis Hassabis have both publicly framed 2026's model releases as the beginning of an AGI era or 'foothills of the singularity.' While treating those claims with appropriate skepticism given the speakers' commercial interests, he stakes out his own more measured position -- that systems capable of a substantial share of today's computer-based knowledge work are likely to arrive within currently-enrolled students' educational lifetimes, though the stronger claim that AI will soon do all such work remains unproven -- and grounds this in evidence like METR's documented growth in AI-agent task duration and DeepMind's AlphaEvolve improving the very training processes underlying itself. The piece's most concrete educational concern is what it calls the 'apprenticeship problem': if AI increasingly performs the preliminary analysis junior professionals traditionally used to build expertise on, 'people will supervise the AI' is an incomplete answer unless institutions explain how those people become qualified supervisors in the first place. Bauschard also raises a philosophical stake -- comparing AGI's potential effect on humanity's self-understanding to the disruptions caused by Copernicus and Darwin -- while grounding the practical decision-making stakes in a 2025 Microsoft study where an AI diagnostic system reached 80-85.5% accuracy on difficult medical cases against a 20% average for generalist physicians. The piece closes with concrete, audience-specific conversation scripts for faculty, students, parents, and trustees, plus a detailed 75-minute meeting structure institutions can run immediately.
points: Bauschard names the 'apprenticeship problem' precisely: if AI increasingly performs the preliminary analysis that used to train junior professionals, 'people will supervise the AI' is incomplete unless institutions can explain how those people acquire the expertise needed to supervise it in the first place.

The Microsoft diagnostic-AI study (80-85.5% accuracy versus a 20% average for generalist physicians on difficult cases) is used not to argue AI should replace human judgment, but to sharpen the harder governance question underneath performance gains: who chooses the objective, who bears the cost of an error, and how can a decision be challenged.

The Copernicus/Darwin analogy is deployed carefully -- not as evidence that today's AGI claims carry the same evidentiary weight as evolutionary biology, but to argue education needs 'a more durable account of human worth than cognitive rank' before a nonhuman system can reliably outperform people at tasks long used to measure human value.

The essay converts abstract institutional anxiety into a specific, reusable 75-minute meeting agenda (shared evidence, a real task walkthrough, three-scenario small-group planning, open disagreement, and concrete committed actions), making the piece as much a leadership tool as an argument.
quotes: At the GPT-6 Astra launch, Greg Brockman declared, "Welcome to the AGI era." OpenAI's president suggested that, looking back in a few years, people might identify this moment and this model as the arrival of AGI.

I think systems capable of performing a substantial share of today's computer-based knowledge work are likely to arrive within the educational lives of students already enrolled. That is my judgment about the direction of the evidence. The stronger claim that AI will soon do all such work remains unproven.

There is an apprenticeship problem here. If AI performs the preliminary analysis that used to train junior professionals, how do beginners acquire the expertise needed to evaluate advanced work? "People will supervise the AI" is an incomplete answer unless we explain how those people become qualified to supervise it.

AI could force a comparably unsettling reconsideration of our intellectual place in the world. It does mean education needs a more durable account of human worth than cognitive rank. A child's value cannot depend on outperforming software.

Depending on its configuration, the system achieved 80% to 85.5% accuracy, compared with a 20% average for the generalist physicians in that experimental comparison. Suppose AI becomes demonstrably better at particular diagnostic decisions.
They are choosing courses now. Families are paying tuition now. Faculty are designing programs now. Donors are deciding what future to support now. Are you ready to have the conversation with them?
